structure.overview: This case concerns an appeal by the Crown against a stay of proceedings granted due to alleged unreasonable delay violating the accused's s. 11(b) Charter right to a trial within a reasonable time. The respondent, Mr. Jacques-Taylor, was charged jointly with a co-accused, and delays arose primarily from the co-accused counsel's unavailability, raising issues about attributing delay and exceptional circumstances in joint trials. The Supreme Court allowed the Crown's appeal, finding that co-accused delay can be a discrete exceptional circumstance but that the Crown failed to take reasonable steps to mitigate delay, ultimately dismissing the appeal and upholding the stay.

summaries.summary: Exceptional circumstances must be unforeseen or unavoidable and Crown must take reasonable steps to avoid delay; success not required, only reasonableness.

citations.why: Defines exceptional circumstances
Requires reasonable steps by Crown

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Crown must mitigate delay from exceptional circumstances and prioritize faltering cases; mitigable delay not subtracted from total delay.

citations.why: Crown's duty to mitigate delay

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: If Crown shows discrete unforeseen event caused delay and took reasonable steps, that delay is subtracted from total time under Jordan's quantitative approach.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Crown argues co-accused delay is a discrete exceptional circumstance, generally unforeseen and unavoidable, and Crown could not have avoided delay here.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Crown contends defence conduct shows Crown reasonably assumed defence accepted pace due to late s. 11(b) filing and no severance request.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Jacques-Taylor argues joint trials should not harm s. 11(b) rights; co-accused delay is within Crown's control and not an exceptional circumstance.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Jacques-Taylor argues the Crown failed to take reasonable steps to address delay after trial dates were assigned, noting defence never waived s. 11(b) rights.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court agrees co-accused scheduling delay can be an exceptional circumstance if unforeseeable and unremediable, citing Jordan para 69.

citations.why: Defines exceptional circumstances test for delay

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court rejects Ontario Court of Appeal's added preconditions for exceptional circumstances in joint trials from R. v. Tran as unnecessary.

citations.why: Rejects added preconditions for exceptional circumstances

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court holds joint trials are presumed in the interests of justice, so Crown need not prove this each time for scheduling delay claims.

citations.cite: R. v. Chow, 2005 SCC 24, [2005] 1 S.C.R. 384, at para. 47
citations.why: Supports presumption that joint trials are in interests of justice

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court states no special rule for joint trials; delay must be unforeseeable or unavoidable and unremediable to qualify as exceptional.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court explains severance to avoid delay is generally unreasonable due to risks and system preference for joint trials, except in complex cases.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court cautions that co-accused delay is not automatically exceptional; Crown must prove exceptional circumstances under Jordan.

citations.cite: R. v. Dos Santos, 2025 ONCA 598, 178 O.R. (3d) 481, at para. 35
citations.why: Supports Crown's burden to prove exceptional circumstances

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court emphasizes the Crown alone must take reasonable steps to address exceptional circumstances causing delay.

citations.why: States Crown's obligation to avoid delay

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Crown argues its reasonable steps depend on defence's s. 11(b) application timing and absence of application implies accused's contentment.

citations.why: Crown's argument on accused's failure to apply affecting reasonable steps

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Crown contends it must rely on accused to signal s. 11(b) jeopardy level, as accused has information Crown lacks.

citations.why: Crown's argument on accused's role in signaling delay

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court disagrees, holding Crown's obligation to take reasonable steps does not depend on accused's s. 11(b) assertion timing.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court explains Jordan shifts burden to Crown after ceiling, requiring Crown to prove exceptional circumstances and reasonable steps, not defence action.

citations.why: Explains Jordan's burden-shifting framework
States Crown's burden to justify delay exceeding ceiling

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court rejects Crown's view that accused's inaction excuses Crown's duty to mitigate delay exceeding the ceiling under Jordan.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court holds Crown does not need accused's input to assess s. 11(b) jeopardy because Jordan's ceilings make delay presumptively unreasonable.

citations.why: Defines presumptive unreasonableness after 18 months

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court states only clear and unequivocal waiver permits inferring accused's contentment with delay; silence or inaction is insufficient.

citations.why: Defines waiver standard
Confirms silence is not waiver
Supports no waiver by silence

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court warns that Crown's approach would encourage complacency Jordan sought to prevent by requiring proactive delay mitigation.

citations.why: Explains need for proactive delay prevention

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court rejects Crown's suggestion that accused's failure to seek severance supports reasonableness of joint trial decision due to rarity of severance.

citations.why: Supports joint trials as norm, severance as exception

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court notes reasonable steps vary; sometimes Crown cannot remedy delay but still meets burden if it shows so.

citations.why: Defines reasonable steps requirement

citations.cite: R. v. Loiacono, 2023 ABCA 157, at para. 28
citations.why: Example where Crown met reasonable steps burden

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court states accused must act diligently but s. 11(b) right is constitutional and only clear waiver or defence delay reduces it.

citations.why: Defines waiver and defence delay requirements

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court finds Crown failed to take reasonable steps to address co-accused counsel unavailability delay, acting too late.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court holds Mr. Jacques-Taylor's missed filing deadline does not excuse Crown's inaction or count as defence delay.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court states Crown must act once ceiling is breached; accused's missed deadline is not clear waiver or excuse for Crown's inaction.

citations.why: Framework for delay ceiling and reasonable steps

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court affirms trial judges can set s. 11(b) application deadlines to prevent delay and expedite trials, citing R. v. Varennes.

citations.cite: R. v. Varennes, 2025 SCC 22, at paras. 82, 86 and 103-5
citations.why: Supports use of deadlines to prevent delay

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court states filing deadlines are important; missed deadlines causing delay can be defence delay, but here no delay was caused by missed deadline.

citations.cite: R. v. Bird, 2019 SCC 7, [2019] 1 S.C.R. 409, at para. 1
citations.why: Supports obligation to follow court orders

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court concludes Crown did not meet burden to take reasonable steps or show inability to do so and dismisses the appeal.
